notes.b: Soups are grouped by their thickness and by the temperature they are served at. Knowing the class tells you what the soup is like and how it is made, and each class has typical examples.
points: Clear (thin) soups are thin and transparent. Consommé is a clear soup made from clarified stock, which is stock cleared of cloudy particles using egg white and minced meat.
Broths are thin, clear soups made by simmering meat or vegetables in water, such as chicken broth or vegetable broth.
Purée soups are thick soups in which cooked vegetables are sieved or blended to a smooth texture, for example carrot, or leek and potato. The vegetables themselves make the soup thick.
Thickened soups are thickened with an added agent such as a roux (a cooked mixture of fat and flour), cornflour, puréed potato, or a liaison, which is a mixture of egg yolk and cream.
Cold soups are served chilled. Gazpacho is a Spanish cold soup of raw tomato, pepper and cucumber.
Stock is the base of most soups. It is a liquid made by simmering bones, meat or vegetables with herbs in water, and it gives the soup its flavour.
To make a good stock, skim off the scum that rises to the surface, do not boil it hard, and strain it at the end so that the finished liquid is clear.
notes.tip: Clear soups and broths are thin, not thick, so a true/false statement calling them thick soups is false. A liaison is a thickener, so a statement saying that is true. For a class-and-example question, name the class, then give one example such as consommé, purée soup or gazpacho.

notes.b: Most soups follow the same order: prepare the vegetables, soften them, add liquid and simmer, then finish. Each step has a reason, which is what examiners look for.
points: Wash, peel and cut the vegetables into even pieces so that they all cook at the same rate and none is left hard or turned to mush.
Sweating the vegetables means to cook them gently in a little fat in a covered pan until soft, without browning, to release their flavour.
Add the stock or liquid, bring the soup to the boil, then simmer until the vegetables are tender. Boiling hard breaks up the vegetables and loses flavour. Thicken the soup if needed.
Purée soups are sieved or blended until smooth. If using a blender, do not overfill it and hold the lid down, because hot liquid can force the lid off.
After puréeing, reheat the soup and season it. Add seasoning at the end and taste first, because the flavour concentrates as the soup reduces and cooks also season in stages.
Add cream, milk or a liaison (egg yolk and cream) off the boil so that the soup does not curdle. Adjust the consistency at the end too.
For safe practice, cool and chill leftover soup quickly, and reheat it until piping hot.
notes.tip: If asked why vegetables are cut evenly, say so they cook at the same rate. If asked why you simmer rather than boil hard, say that fierce boiling breaks up the vegetables and loses flavour.

notes.b: A soup is served at the right temperature and finished with a garnish, a small decoration added for colour and flavour. The garnish and bowl are chosen to suit the type of soup.
points: Serve hot soup hot and in warm bowls so that it does not cool quickly. Thick soups are garnished with croutons, chopped parsley or chives, a swirl of cream or grated cheese.
Clear soups are garnished with thin strips of vegetable or chopped herbs, which keep the soup looking light and clear.
Cold soups are chilled thoroughly before serving and garnished with finely diced vegetables or a little cream.
A garnish must be edible, suit the soup and be small. Accompaniments, such as brown bread, are served alongside.
notes.tip: Croutons are a garnish for soup, and a true/false question may ask this. Give examples that suit the soup, such as croutons on a thick soup and thin vegetable strips on a clear soup.

notes.h: Making a roux and a roux-based sauce
notes.b: A roux is a cooked mixture of equal amounts of fat and flour (by weight), and the amount of liquid added decides the thickness of the sauce. Changing the liquid, not the roux, gives different sauces.
points: 1. Melt the fat. 2. Stir in an equal amount of flour and cook gently, briefly, to remove the raw flour taste. 3. Add the liquid gradually, stirring or whisking so that the starch disperses without lumps.
4. Bring the sauce to the boil, then simmer it to cook the starch fully. 5. Season.
A roux thickens because the starch granules absorb liquid and swell as the sauce heats, a process called gelatinisation.
A white roux is cooked only briefly, until pale. It thickens most strongly and is used for white, parsley, cheese, mushroom and béchamel sauces.
A brown roux is cooked longer until golden or brown. It thickens less and is used for brown and stewing sauces.

The same fat and flour give thin pouring, thicker coating and very thick binding sauces by using progressively less liquid: more for a pouring sauce, less for a coating sauce, least for a binding sauce (panada).
Béchamel is a white sauce made by infusing milk with flavourings such as onion, bay leaf and cloves. Panada is a thick, roux-based paste used to bind ingredients such as croquettes.
Roux-based sauces accepted as examples are white, parsley, béchamel, cheese, mushroom, curry, stewing, panada and brown sauce.
notes.tip: A roux always has equal fat and flour. The amount of liquid changes the sauce, not the amount of roux ingredients. Béchamel is made with infused milk, so do not call it a cream sauce; white sauce is the same method without the infusion. To describe a roux sauce, give equal fat and flour with liquid added, with an example such as white, cheese or parsley sauce.

notes.h: Classes of sauce and their examples
notes.b: Besides roux-based sauces, sauces are classified by what thickens or makes them, or by how they are served. Examiners ask for a class with an example, so learn one or two for each.
points: Roux-based sauces: white, parsley, cheese, mushroom, béchamel, curry and stewing sauce.
Egg-based sauces: custard sets because egg proteins coagulate in hot milk. Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil in egg yolk, and hollandaise is an emulsion of butter in egg yolk with lemon juice.
Sweet sauces: chocolate, toffee, caramel and butterscotch, served with desserts.
Fruit sauces: apple sauce, orange sauce and coulis, a thin purée of raw or cooked fruit, often sieved.
Cold sauces and dressings: mint sauce and French dressing, which are served cold.
Miscellaneous sauces: bread sauce, thickened with breadcrumbs.
Uses: white sauce with fish, cheese sauce with cauliflower, apple sauce with pork, mint sauce with lamb, custard with apple tart and French dressing on salad.
notes.tip: Mayonnaise is under egg-based in one marking scheme and under cold sauces in another. Give it under egg based and mention that it is also served cold. For one roux, one egg-based and one sweet sauce, you could give white sauce, custard and chocolate sauce.

notes.b: Convenience soups are ready-made soups that save preparation time. They come in five forms, and each is stored and prepared differently.
points: Dehydrated or packaged soups are dried mixes reconstituted with boiling water or milk. They have a long shelf life.
Cook-chill soups are sold chilled and heated before eating. They have a shorter shelf life than canned soups.
Canned soups are sterilised in sealed tins, which gives a long shelf life, and they only need heating.
Frozen soups are stored at −18 °C and heated after thawing. They keep their flavour well.
Single-portion soups are sold in individual pots or cups that are heated or reconstituted for one serving.
notes.tip: When outlining the range, name all five: dehydrated or packaged, cook-chill, canned, frozen and single-portion. Do not say a cook-chill soup lasts longer than a canned one.

notes.h: Advantages and disadvantages of convenience soups
notes.b: Convenience soups trade cost and quality for speed and ease. Weigh them against homemade soup when you evaluate them.
points: Advantages: little preparation time, simple skills needed, useful in an emergency, wide variety available, and easy to store. Dried and canned soups also have a long shelf life.
Disadvantages: they can be expensive per portion, are often high in salt, and may contain artificial colours, flavours and additives.
They may also have less fibre and flavour than homemade soup, and you have less choice over the ingredients used.
Adding fresh vegetables, herbs, milk or a topping to a convenience soup improves its flavour and adds nutrients.
notes.tip: Questions usually ask for three advantages and three disadvantages. Pick distinct points, such as quick, easy to store and wide variety, against expensive, high in salt and contains additives.

notes.b: Labels let a consumer compare soups and choose for health or allergy needs. Labelling rules for food are set by Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
points: The label must give the name of the food, the ingredients list, and the net quantity in metric units.
Ingredients are listed in descending order of weight at the time of manufacture, so the first ingredient is the one used in greatest amount.
Allergenic ingredients, such as gluten, milk, eggs, celery and nuts, must be emphasised within the ingredients list so that people with allergies can spot them.
The nutrition declaration gives energy and the amounts of fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt per 100 g or 100 ml.
Cooking instructions, storage conditions and a use-by or best-before date are shown.
The name and address of the food business operator are given, along with the country of origin where it is required.
Labels let the consumer compare soups by salt content, ingredients and allergens, and check that the soup suits their needs.
notes.tip: For the role of labelling for a consumer, give three points and explain each, such as ingredients, nutrition information, date marks, allergens, and storage and cooking instructions. A short list of manufacturer details also scores: name, ingredients, quantity in metric units, nutritional content, cooking instructions, storage, best-before date and manufacturer.

keyTerms.definition: A cooked mixture of equal amounts of fat and flour, used to thicken sauces and soups.
A thickening mixture of egg yolk and cream stirred into a hot soup or sauce.
Cooked food sieved or blended to a smooth, thick texture.
A clear soup made from stock clarified with egg white and minced meat.
A flavoured liquid made by simmering bones, meat or vegetables in water with herbs.
Cooking vegetables gently in a little fat in a covered pan until soft, without colouring them.
A mixture of two liquids that do not normally blend, such as oil and egg yolk, held together by an emulsifier.
A thin, sieved purée of raw or cooked fruit or vegetables, used as a sauce.
A cold Spanish soup made from raw tomato, pepper and cucumber.
A ready-made soup that needs little or no preparation before it is served.
A method of cooking food, chilling it quickly and storing it under refrigeration until it is reheated.

factCards.definition: Clear soups, such as consommé, and broths.
Dehydrated or packaged, cook-chill, canned, frozen, and single-portion.
High salt content; artificial colours and flavours; additives.

factCards.term: Two reasons a roux is cooked before liquid is added
factCards.definition: To remove the raw flour taste, and to allow the starch to thicken the liquid smoothly.

questions.prompt: Explain how a white roux is made and name two sauces made from it.
questions.model: Melt the fat and stir in an equal amount of flour; cook the mixture briefly until pale to remove the raw flour taste. Add the liquid gradually, stirring or whisking to prevent lumps, then bring to the boil and simmer until the starch has thickened the sauce. Any two sauces: white sauce, parsley sauce, cheese sauce, béchamel, mushroom sauce.

questions.prompt: Classify soups into thin, thick and cold classes, giving an example of each. Then outline the advantages and disadvantages of convenience soups for a busy household, and state two pieces of information a consumer should check on the label.
questions.model: Thin soups: clear soups such as consommé, and broths such as chicken or vegetable broth. Thick soups: purées such as carrot or leek and potato, and thickened soups made with a roux, cornflour or a liaison of egg yolk and cream. Cold soups: gazpacho, a Spanish soup of raw tomato, pepper and cucumber, chilled before serving. Advantages of convenience soups: little preparation time; simple skills needed; useful in an emergency; wide variety; easy to store. Disadvantages: expensive per portion; often high in salt; artificial colours, flavours and additives may be present. Label checks, any two: the ingredients list, with allergens emphasised; the salt and nutrition declaration; the net quantity; the use-by or best-before date; the storage and cooking instructions; whether any ingredient is genetically modified or irradiated.
